name: Message Queues
intent: Let one part of a system hand work to another without waiting for it, by putting messages in a durable line that workers take from at their own pace.
scenario: When a customer checks out, the shop must send a confirmation email, update stock and notify the warehouse. The email provider is slow and sometimes down, but checkout should stay fast.
problem: If checkout calls each service directly and waits, it is as slow as the slowest one, and it fails when any of them fails. A burst of orders can also overwhelm a downstream service that can only handle so much at once. The sender and receiver are tied together in time.

howItWorks.title: The producer enqueues and moves on
howItWorks.text: Checkout writes a small message ('send email for order 42') to the queue and immediately continues. The queue stores it durably, so the message survives restarts, and delivery no longer needs the receiver to be up right now.

howItWorks.title: Consumers take messages when they are ready
howItWorks.text: Workers pull messages from the queue, process them, and acknowledge each one when done. A slow or busy worker takes fewer messages, so the queue absorbs bursts and smooths the load (this is called load levelling).

howItWorks.title: Unacknowledged messages are redelivered
howItWorks.text: If a worker crashes before acknowledging, the queue hands the message to another worker. Delivery is therefore usually at least once: a message can arrive twice, so handlers should be idempotent (safe to run twice, with the same result as running once).

howItWorks.title: Many consumers share the work
howItWorks.text: Several workers can read from the same queue (competing consumers). Each message goes to exactly one of them, so adding workers raises throughput without changing the producer.

howItWorks.title: Failures need a plan: retries and a dead-letter queue
howItWorks.text: A message that keeps failing (a poison message) is retried a limited number of times, often with a growing delay, and then moved to a dead-letter queue for a human to inspect, so it cannot block everything behind it.

pros: Producers stay fast and keep working while consumers are slow or down
Absorbs traffic bursts and protects downstream services
Decouples services in time and in knowledge of each other
cons: Work becomes asynchronous: the caller does not get the result immediately
At-least-once delivery means duplicates, so handlers must be idempotent
Ordering is limited and message loss, poison messages and backlogs must be handled
Another system to run and monitor
whenToUse: Work that does not need to finish before replying: emails, image processing, reports
Calling a slow or unreliable service
Spiky load that a downstream system cannot absorb directly
Spreading jobs across a pool of workers
whenNotToUse: The caller needs the answer now (use a direct call)
Strict global ordering across all messages is essential
A simple function call or database row would do and queueing adds no value
pitfalls: Assuming exactly-once delivery: design for duplicates instead
No dead-letter queue, so one bad message loops forever
An ever-growing queue that nobody monitors until it is hours behind
Putting large payloads in messages instead of a reference to them

roles.label: Queue
roles.description: Stores messages durably until they are acknowledged.

quiz.question: A photo app creates thumbnails inside the upload request. When a user uploads a large image, the request takes 8 seconds and sometimes times out under bursts. Which change best fixes this?
options: Raise the client timeout to 30 seconds so large uploads can finish
Enqueue a thumbnail job and return to the user immediately
Run the thumbnail code on more web servers to handle the bursts
Cache the thumbnails so that repeated uploads are faster
quiz.explanation: The user does not need the thumbnail before the upload is confirmed, so a queue lets the request finish at once and workers process jobs at their own pace. A longer timeout or more web servers keeps the slow work in the request path, and a cache does nothing for the first upload of each image.

quiz.question: A payment worker charges the card, then crashes before acknowledging the queue message. The queue redelivers it, and the customer is charged twice. The queue promises at-least-once delivery. What is the best fix?
options: Acknowledge each message as soon as it arrives, before charging
Turn on exactly-once delivery and remove the other checks
Run a single consumer so a message is never seen twice
Make the handler idempotent with a unique payment key
quiz.explanation: At-least-once delivery means duplicates will happen, so the handler must be safe to run twice. Acknowledging first swaps duplicates for lost payments when a worker crashes mid-charge, and one consumer still sees redelivery after a crash.

quiz.question: One message with a malformed payload makes the consumer crash every time. The queue redelivers it immediately, workers keep restarting, and two hours of backlog build up behind it. What is the best fix?
options: Limit retries with backoff, then move it to a dead-letter queue
Add more consumers so the other messages can get past it
Make the queue's visibility timeout much longer for all messages
Delete a message silently after its first failed attempt
quiz.explanation: A poison message needs a retry limit and a dead-letter queue so a human can inspect it while healthy messages continue. A longer visibility timeout (how long a taken message stays hidden) only delays the same retry. More consumers crash on it in turn, and silently deleting it loses data that may matter.
